## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a safe, observable canary rollout using standard Kubernetes resources and NGINX Ingress without a service mesh.

## Key Concepts
- Canary deployment pattern with separate Deployments
- Ingress annotations (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary, canary-weight)
- Progressive traffic shifting and rollback strategy
- Observability: latency, error rate, saturation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Stable Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: stable
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: stable
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: stable
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend-canary
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: canary
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:1.2-canary
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml
# Ingress (production path)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: frontend-ingress
  namespace: prod
  annotations:
    # enable canary routing for the canary backend
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: "frontend.example.com"
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: frontend-canary
            port:
              number: 80
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to design an isolated TLS rotation workflow that leverages cert-manager, RBAC, and policy enforcement while producing auditable logs.

## Key Concepts
- Deployments, InitContainers, and probes for reliable pod lifecycle management
- Secrets and Bearer token authentication for secure credential handling
- cert-manager integration for automated certificate rotation testing
- PVC-based logging for persistent audit trails
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control and network segmentation

## Trade-offs
- **Simplicity vs. Security**: Using a single ServiceAccount with broad permissions simplifies implementation but increases blast radius if compromised
- **PVC vs. Sidecar**: A sidecar container offers simpler log shipping but adds resource overhead; a PVC requires external log rotation
- **Polling vs. Watching**: Polling with a cron-style schedule is less efficient than watching but avoids the complexity of setting up a custom controller with informers
- **Egress Control**: NetworkPolicy adds security but increases operational complexity and requires CNI support

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["cert-manager.io"]
    resources: ["certificates"]
    verbs: ["get", "create", "delete"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: cert-verifier
    namespace: cert-verifier
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: cert-verifier
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-credentials
  namespace: cert-verifier
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: "<bearer-token>"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier-logs
  namespace: cert-verifier
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cert-verifier
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cert-verifier
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: cert-verifier
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: alpine:latest
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - apk add --no-cache curl jq
          volumeMounts:
            - name: workdir
              mountPath: /work
      containers:
        - name: verifier
          image: alpine:latest
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              apk add --no-cache curl jq
              while true; do
                # Watch secrets, check expiry, rotate, post digest
                sleep 3600
              done
          volumeMounts:
            - name: workdir
              mountPath: /work
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthy
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: workdir
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: cert-verifier-logs
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier-egress
  namespace: cert-verifier
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cert-verifier
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              name: audit-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: audit-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical hardening: container securityContext, readiness/liveness, graceful shutdown, high-availability with PDB, and network isolation via NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts
- Pod securityContext and container securityContext
- Probes and lifecycle hooks
- PodDisruptionBudget
- NetworkPolicy basics and egress constraints
- Per-namespace isolation in production-grade CKAD

## Code Example
```javascript
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: secure
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: api:latest
        securityContext:
          runAsUser: 10001
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/api-config
        - name: secret
          mountPath: /etc/api-secret
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 8080
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: api-config
      - name: secret
        secret:
          secretName: api-secret
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api-pdb
  namespace: secure
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-egress
  namespace: secure
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
      ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.96.0.0/12
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  - to:

    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of InitContainer lifecycle, idempotent seeding patterns, and persistent cache management across pod restarts.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainers and startup ordering
- ConfigMap-based seed script injection
- PVC-backed shared cache for idempotence
- Marker file pattern for preventing re-seeding
- Readiness and liveness probe configuration
- Load testing and rollback strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
# Seed script ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: seed-scripts
data:
  seed.sh: |
    #!/bin/sh
    set -e
    if [ ! -f /cache/.seeded ]; then
      # Execute seeding logic here
      touch /cache/.seeded
    fi
---
# Deployment with InitContainer
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-server
  namespace: ckad
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: seed-cache
        image: busybox:1.35
        command: ['/bin/sh', '/scripts/seed.sh']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: seed-scripts
          mountPath: /scripts
        - name: cache-volume
          mountPath: /cache
      containers:
      - name: api-server
        image: api-server:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: cache-volume
          mountPath: /cache
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: seed-scripts
        configMap:
          name: seed-scripts
      - name: cache-volume
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: cache-pvc
```

## Verification Strategy
1. **Load Testing**: Use kubectl exec to simulate concurrent requests, monitor cache seeding behavior, and verify marker file prevents re-seeding
2. **Rollback Approach**: Deploy with strategy type RollingUpdate, set maxUnavailable and maxSurge for controlled rollout, and use kubectl rollout undo if issues arise
3. **Monitoring**: Check InitContainer logs, verify probe status, and confirm cache persistence across pod restarts

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates comprehensive understanding of Kubernetes backup strategies, per-namespace automation patterns, and production-ready deployment practices. It tests the ability to coordinate multiple Kubernetes resources while maintaining proper isolation and observability.

## Key Concepts
- VolumeSnapshot API integration with VolumeSnapshotClass configuration
- Per-namespace CronJob deployment with appropriate RBAC boundaries
- ConfigMap-based state management for backup status tracking
- PVC-backed logging infrastructure with InitContainer tool deployment
- Namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy implementation for egress control
- Operational considerations including cadence optimization and retention policies

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: backup-scheduler
  namespace: {{ .Release.Namespace }}
spec:
  schedule: "0 0/12 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: install-tools
            image: busybox:1.35
            command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache velero jq']
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: velero/velero:latest
            command: ['sh', '-c', 'velero snapshot create --from-pvc app-data && kubectl create configmap backup-status --from-literal=status=completed --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -']
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ['pgrep', 'velero']
              initialDelaySeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ['pgrep', 'velero']
              initialDelaySeconds: 30
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: backup-logs
```

## Trade-offs Discussion
**Frequency vs. Resource Consumption**: 12-hour intervals balance data protection requirements against cluster resource utilization and storage costs.

**Per-namespace vs. Cluster-wide**: Namespace-scoped deployment provides better isolation but increases operational complexity compared to a centralized backup controller.

**Storage Considerations**: VolumeSnapshot API offers efficient storage but requires compatible storage classes and may incur additional costs based on provider pricing models.

**Network Policy Impact**: Egress restrictions enhance security but may complicate troubleshooting and require careful endpoint whitelisting.

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to translate dynamic allowlists into enforced Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules while maintaining per-namespace isolation. It combines ConfigMap-driven configuration, DNS resolution, RBAC scoping, and observability—all core CKAD competencies.

## Key Concepts

- **NetworkPolicy**: Enforces egress rules at the pod level using `ipBlock` selectors. Note that egress rules require CNI support for enforcement.
- **ConfigMap**: Serves as the externalized allowlist store, allowing updates without pod or job restarts.
- **CronJob**: Periodically reconciles the allowlist state with the active NetworkPolicy, acting as a controller loop.
- **InitContainer**: Ensures required tools are available before the main container starts, though using a pre-built image with curl is simpler.
- **PVC**: Provides persistent storage for test results, enabling post-job analysis and debugging.

## Common Pitfalls

- Forgetting DNS egress rules causes complete name resolution failure
- Using `0.0.0.0/0` with broad `except` blocks can create confusing policies
- Resolving hostnames to IPs at apply time introduces a lag between DNS changes and policy updates
- Not all CNIs fully support egress policies; test enforcement in your target environment

## Production Considerations

- Add error handling and alerting for resolution failures
- Consider using a mutating webhook or operator for more robust reconciliation
- Implement metric export (Prometheus) for monitoring resolution success rates
- Add retry logic with exponential backoff for transient network failures

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical CKAD skills: wiring ConfigMaps and Secrets, configuring InitContainers, implementing TLS sidecars, setting up readiness/liveness probes, and crafting a NetworkPolicy with conditional egress.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven feature flags
- Secrets for credential management
- InitContainers for tooling installation
- TLS sidecars for secure communication
- Readiness and liveness probe configuration
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: feature-config
data:
  ENABLE_API: "true"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: api-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  token: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: app-namespace
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-policy
  namespace: app-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: internal-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: app-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: curlimages/curl:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo Initialized']
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: my-app:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: ENABLE_API
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: feature-config
                  key: ENABLE_API
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: api-creds
                  key: token
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /status
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /status
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
        - name: tls-sidecar
          image: nginx:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 443
```

## Trade-offs
- **NetworkPolicy complexity**: The policy above allows egress only to the internal-api pod. A more permissive approach might allow DNS resolution but restrict target services.
- **InitContainer overhead**: Installing curl in every pod increases startup time and image size. Consider baking tools into the base image if startup latency is critical.
- **Sidecar maintenance**: A TLS sidecar adds complexity and resource overhead. For simple use cases, TLS could be handled within the application container directly.
- **Secret security**: Storing credentials in a Secret is fine for basic scenarios, but consider external secrets operators or vault integration for production environments requiring rotation.
- **Probe configuration**: Aggressive probe settings can cause unnecessary restarts; conservative settings may delay failure detection. Tune based on application startup time.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical knowledge of namespace-scoped governance primitives and their impact on scheduling, pod density, and autoscaler behavior.

## Key Concepts
- **ResourceQuota** enforces hard caps on total namespace resource consumption (CPU, memory, pod count, etc.)
- **LimitRange** sets defaults and constraints for individual pod/container resource requests and limits
- Quota enforcement affects scheduler decisions, pod scheduling failures, and autoscaler calculations
- Use `kubectl describe resourcequota <name> --namespace=<ns>` and `kubectl top pod` to monitor usage

## Code Example

```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: quota-demo
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: ns-quota
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
    pods: "20"
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: ns-limits
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 250m
      memory: 256Mi
    max:
      cpu: "2"
      memory: "4Gi"
    min:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
---
# Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: quota-demo-app
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 128Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 512Mi
```

## Trade-offs
- **Flexibility vs. Control**: Quotas prevent resource hoarding but require developers to specify requests/limits, increasing YAML complexity
- **Utilization Risk**: Overly restrictive quotas lead to pod scheduling failures; overly generous quotas waste resources
- **Debugging Overhead**: Quota-induced failures (e.g., "pods quota exceeded") add a layer of complexity to troubleshooting
- **Autoscaler Interaction**: VPA/HPA behavior changes when quotas constrain available headroom
